title: The way to Brahma
hook: Subha asks about householder and renunciant; the four immeasurables as the way to Brahma

segments.voice: Yesterday: preserving truth. Say this is my faith, not only this is true. Your line was preserve the truth. Where did you say I believe? Day four hundred seventy-seven, a new week.

A young brahmin named Subha is staying in Sāvatthī on business. He comes to the Buddha with a question that still turns up at kitchen tables. Who does better, the person who stays in the world, with a job and a family, or the person who leaves it all for a spiritual life? The brahmins of his day, he says, hold that the householder is the one who accomplishes what is good. What does the Buddha say? He answers by refusing to give a one-word answer.
screen: `SUBHA, IN TOWN ON BUSINESS.` → `THE HOUSEHOLDER OR THE ONE WHO LEAVES?` → `NO ONE-WORD ANSWER.`

segments.voice: On this, the Buddha says, I'm one who analyzes; I don't speak one-sidedly. A householder who lives badly doesn't accomplish the good, and neither does a monk who lives badly. A householder or a monk who lives well, either can. Then the conversation turns to Brahmā, the high god the brahmins hoped to be united with after death. Subha has heard that the Buddha knows the way to companionship with Brahmā. The Buddha says: suppose a man was born and raised in a village called Naḷakāra, not far from here. If someone asked him the way to Naḷakāra, would he hesitate? No, he grew up there. In the same way, the Buddha says, I know Brahmā and the way there. So Subha asks: teach me the way. And the Buddha describes four states of heart. A person fills one direction with a mind of loving-kindness, then the second, the third, the fourth, then above, below, across, everywhere, a mind abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility. Then compassion, the same way. Then appreciative joy, gladness at others' good. Then equanimity. These are the four immeasurables, also called the brahmavihāras, the dwellings of Brahmā. When the heart is freed like this, the Buddha says, no limited action remains there. And he gives a picture: a strong conch-blower makes himself heard in all four directions without effort. That's the way to Brahmā in this sutta: not a ritual, not a birth, but a heart grown so wide it has no edges. Subha leaves delighted, and goes for refuge.
screen: `ONE WHO ANALYZES, NOT ONE-SIDED.` · `BORN IN NAḶAKĀRA.` · `FOUR DIRECTIONS, ABOVE, BELOW, EVERYWHERE.` · `THE CONCH-BLOWER.` · then, large: `THE WAY TO BRAHMA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: practice one immeasurable. Sit and settle. Choose one: kindness, compassion, gladness at others' good, or steady equanimity. Start with someone easy. Feel it toward them. Then let it spread, the way the sutta says, in one direction, the people in front of you, then behind, to the sides, above and below, until it has no edge. If your mind wanders, start again with the easy person. The bell holds the time.
The way to Brahma. Loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy and equanimity, spread in every direction without limit: the dwellings of Brahmā. Today's word.
Your line: the way to Brahma. Today, pick one immeasurable and send it, silently, in every direction you face. Day four hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: The four brahmavihāras, loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy and equanimity, are practiced across Buddhist traditions, often by radiating each one toward oneself, loved ones, strangers, difficult people and all beings in every direction.

myth: the Buddha says only monks can accomplish the good
he says either can, if they live well, and neither can if they live badly.
the four immeasurables are also called the dwellings of Brahmā
brahmavihāra: the abodes or dwellings of Brahmā.

fork.setup: Subha asks: who does better, the one who stays home or the one who leaves for the spiritual life? what does the Buddha answer?
options: it depends on how each one lives
fork.reveal: 'I'm one who analyzes,' he says. either can live well or badly. the answer isn't in the role but in the life.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit brahmavihāra: dwelling of Brahmā, the name for the four immeasurables.

trapdoor: what you thought: the way to Brahma is a prayer to a god.
what it means: in this sutta, the four immeasurables, a heart of kindness, compassion, joy and equanimity spread in every direction.
what a scholar hears: MN 99, the Subha Sutta; the Buddha calls himself vibhajjavāda, 'one who analyzes', a word later taken up by the Theravada as a name for its own approach.

notes: MN 99 paraphrased; check the 'one who analyzes' reply, the Naḷakāra village simile, the four immeasurables and the conch-blower.
The sutta's middle section (the five things brahmins prescribe for merit, the 'line of blind men' about Brahmā) is skipped for focus.
Brahmā is described simply as 'the high god the brahmins hoped to be united with'; a Keeper may want a note on Brahmā's place in Buddhist cosmology.
vibhajjavāda as a later Theravada self-description: confirm phrasing.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the unsourced 'a question many people still ask' from the hook. The rest checked against MN 99 as remembered (vibhajjavādo, Naḷakāra, the four immeasurables, the conch-blower); no other changes.
